policy-short-run-s1.title: Sundra in a recession (invented country)
policy-short-run-s1.html: Sundra, an invented country, is in a recession. Real GDP is below full-employment output, and the unemployment rate is 8 percent while the natural rate is 5 percent. Sundra's central bank operates in an ample-reserves framework: it steers its policy rate with the interest rate it pays on reserve balances. Sundra's legislature can also change government spending or taxes.

items.q: Which action by Sundra's central bank would move real GDP back toward full employment?
options: Sell government bonds to drain reserves
Lower the interest rate it pays on reserve balances
Raise the interest rate it pays on reserve balances
Raise the required reserve ratio for banks

items.q: Sundra's central bank lowers the interest rate it pays on reserve balances. Put the links of the chain in order, from the action to the result.
options: The interest rate on reserve balances falls
The policy rate falls
Loan rates and other interest rates fall
Investment and interest-sensitive consumption rise
Aggregate demand shifts right
Real GDP rises and unemployment falls

items.q: Suppose Sundra's legislature cuts personal income taxes instead. What is the first link in the chain from the tax cut to AD?
options: Disposable income rises, so households spend more
The policy rate falls, so firms borrow more
Production costs fall for firms, so SRAS shifts right
Potential output rises, so LRAS shifts right

items.q: Sundra's central bank lowers its administered rates and, at the same time, the legislature raises government spending. Compared with either policy alone, what happens to AD and to the interest rates banks charge on loans?
options: AD rises by more; loan rates fall for sure
AD rises by more; loan rates rise for sure
AD rises by more; the effect on loan rates is indeterminate
The effect on AD is indeterminate, and loan rates fall for sure

items.q: An economy has an inflationary gap, and its central bank operates with ample reserves. Build the chain for the right monetary policy.

specific.frame: The central bank ___ the interest rate on reserve balances, so the policy rate ___. Borrowing costs more, so ___ falls, AD shifts ___, and ___ fall.
specific.model: The central bank raises the interest rate on reserve balances, so the policy rate rises. Borrowing costs more, so investment falls, which shifts AD left, and as a result the price level and real output fall toward full employment.

policy.label: The action
options: raises
lowers

why.1: Lowering it is expansionary; an inflationary gap needs a contractionary move.

rate.label: The policy rate
options: rises
falls

why.1: The policy rate follows the administered rate up.

spending.label: The spending that falls
options: investment
government spending
potential output

why.1: Monetary policy works through interest-sensitive private spending, not the government budget.
why.2: Potential output is set by resources and technology, not by the policy rate.

direction.label: Which way AD shifts
options: left
right

why.1: Less spending at each price level is a shift left.

price.label: What falls
options: the price level and real output
full-employment output

why.1: Full-employment output (LRAS) does not move in the short run; the equilibrium moves along SRAS.

items.q: The graph shows Tolmar after aggregate demand fell from AD1 to AD2. LRAS marks full-employment output. What does the new short-run equilibrium show?
options: An inflationary gap: output is above full employment
No gap: output is still at full employment
A recessionary gap with unemployment below the natural rate
A recessionary gap: output is below full employment

items.q: Which pair of policies would both push AD from AD2 back toward AD1?
options: A rise in taxes and a lower policy rate
A cut in taxes and a lower policy rate
A cut in government spending and a higher policy rate
A rise in government spending and a higher policy rate

items.q: Suppose Tolmar uses no policy at all. What happens to its economy in the long run?
options: Nominal wages rise, SRAS shifts left, and output returns to full employment
LRAS shifts left to meet the lower level of output
Nominal wages fall, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to full employment
AD shifts back right on its own as the price level falls

items.q: Tolmar's recessionary gap is 200 billion dollars and its MPC is 0.75. By how much would government spending have to rise to close the gap, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You multiplied the gap by the multiplier. The multiplier makes each dollar of spending count several times, so divide the gap by it: 200 / 4 = 50.
You divided by the MPC. Divide by the spending multiplier, 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4.

items.q: In which countries do the fiscal and central bank actions push AD in opposite directions? Select all that apply.
options: Bela
Coro
Dren
Esk

items.q: In Coro, what happens to the policy rate, investment and the price level?
options: The policy rate rises, investment rises, the price level rises
The policy rate falls, investment rises, the price level falls
The policy rate is unchanged, investment falls, the price level falls
The policy rate rises, investment falls, the price level falls

items.q: In Bela, which variable's change cannot be determined without knowing the sizes of the two policies?
options: Real output
Interest rates on loans
The price level
The unemployment rate

items.q: Dren's central bank sells government bonds. On which graph is that action shown, and what does it show?
options: The money market: the money supply shifts left and the nominal interest rate rises
The reserve market: the administered rate rises and so does the policy rate
The loanable funds market: the supply of funds shifts right and the real interest rate falls
The money market: money demand shifts right and the nominal interest rate rises

items.q: Ruskel, an invented country, has an inflationary gap: AD crosses SRAS to the right of LRAS. Its central bank, which operates with ample reserves, raises the interest rate on reserve balances. Shift the right curve and mark the new short-run equilibrium.

key.because: a higher policy rate that lowers investment

slips.SRAS: A higher policy rate changes how much firms and households borrow and spend, so it shifts AD; it does not change production costs.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares fiscal and monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fiscal policy shifts AD; monetary policy shifts SRAS through interest costs
Monetary policy shifts AD in limited reserves but LRAS in ample reserves
Both shift AD; fiscal policy works through spending or taxes, monetary policy through interest rates
Both shift LRAS by changing how much the economy can produce

items.q: A rise in government spending raises real GDP and the price level. On the money market graph, what happens, and why?
options: Money supply rises because the government is spending more money, so the nominal interest rate falls
Money demand rises, as more output at higher prices takes more money, so the nominal rate rises
Money demand falls because higher prices make money worth less, so the nominal interest rate falls
Money supply falls because the government borrows from banks, so the nominal interest rate rises

items.q: An economy has an inflationary gap. Select every action that would shift AD to the left.
options: Raising income taxes
Raising the interest rate on reserve balances (ample reserves)
Buying government bonds on the open market (limited reserves)
Raising transfer payments to households

items.q: Label the axes and both curves of the Phillips curve graph.
The economy starts where SRPC crosses LRPC. Then consumer spending rises, shifting AD right. Place point B to show where the economy moves in the short run.
A sharp rise in world oil prices raises production costs for firms across the economy. Shift the right curve to show the effect on the Phillips curves.

key.because: a negative supply shock (higher oil prices)

slips.LRPC: A supply shock does not change the natural rate of unemployment, so LRPC stays where it is. The short-run trade-off gets worse, so SRPC shifts.

items.q: After years of rising prices, workers and firms come to expect a higher inflation rate. Shift the right curve and mark the new long-run equilibrium where the curves cross.

slips.LRPC: Expected inflation changes the short-run trade-off; the natural rate of unemployment, and so LRPC, does not depend on it.

items.q: Between which two years did Velor most likely move along a single short-run Phillips curve after a rise in AD?
options: Year 1 to Year 2
Year 2 to Year 3
Year 3 to Year 4
Year 1 to Year 3

items.q: In Year 3, unemployment is back at the natural rate, but inflation is 4 percent instead of the 2 percent of Year 1. What best explains this?
options: The natural rate of unemployment fell, so LRPC shifted left and inflation rose along it
AD fell, so the economy moved down along the SRPC toward higher inflation
Expected inflation rose, so the SRPC shifted right and the economy returned to LRPC at a higher inflation rate
A positive supply shock shifted the SRPC left, raising inflation

items.q: From Year 3 to Year 4, both unemployment and inflation rose. Which event fits that change?
options: A rise in government spending on roads that shifted AD right
A sharp rise in energy prices that shifted SRAS left
A fall in consumer confidence that shifted AD left
A fall in the natural rate of unemployment

items.q: Using the table, what is Velor's cyclical unemployment rate in Year 4?

mistakes.why: That is the actual unemployment rate. Cyclical unemployment is the part above the natural rate: 6.5 - 5.0.
You added the natural rate. The actual rate is natural plus cyclical, so subtract: 6.5 - 5.0.

items.q: What happens to Lumen's unemployment and inflation rates in the short run?
options: Unemployment rises above 4 percent, and inflation rises above 2 percent
Unemployment falls below 4 percent, and inflation falls below 2 percent
Unemployment stays at 4 percent, and inflation rises above 2 percent
Unemployment falls below 4 percent, and inflation rises above 2 percent

items.q: Households and firms in Lumen come to expect the higher inflation rate. Where does the economy end up in the long run?
options: Below 4 percent unemployment, with inflation back at 2 percent
At 4 percent unemployment, with inflation above 2 percent, on a new SRPC
At 4 percent unemployment, with inflation back down at the old 2 percent
Above 4 percent unemployment, with inflation below 2 percent

items.q: Which change on Lumen's AD-AS graph matches its long-run adjustment?
options: Nominal wages rise with expected inflation, so SRAS shifts left until output is back at full employment
Nominal wages fall, so SRAS shifts right and output rises further above full employment
LRAS shifts right to meet the higher level of output
AD keeps shifting right until the price level stops rising

items.q: Build the chain for Lumen, from the spending boom to the long run.

specific.frame: Consumption rises, so AD shifts ___. Unemployment ___ and inflation rises: a movement ___ the SRPC. As expected inflation rises, the SRPC shifts ___, and unemployment returns to ___.
specific.model: Consumption rises, so AD shifts right. Unemployment falls and inflation rises, which is a movement along the SRPC. Because expected inflation then rises, the SRPC shifts right, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 4 percent.

direction.label: Which way AD shifts
options: right
left

why.1: More consumption is more spending at each price level: a shift right.

unemployment.label: Unemployment in the short run
options: falls
rises

why.1: Higher output needs more workers, so unemployment falls.

link.label: Movement or shift
options: along
of

why.1: An AD change moves the economy along the SRPC; it does not shift it.

curve.label: Which way the SRPC shifts
options: right
left

why.1: Higher expected inflation raises inflation at each unemployment rate: a shift right (up).

trend.label: The long-run unemployment rate
options: the natural rate of 4 percent
a rate below 4 percent

why.1: LRPC is vertical at the natural rate; unemployment cannot stay below it in the long run.

items.q: Better job-search websites help unemployed workers find matching jobs faster, so the natural rate of unemployment falls. Shift the right curve.

key.because: a fall in the natural rate of unemployment

items.q: The economy starts where SRPC crosses LRPC. Then business investment falls sharply, shifting AD left. Place point B to show the short-run result.
What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve show?
options: In the long run, higher inflation keeps unemployment permanently lower
In the long run, the inflation rate is fixed whatever the unemployment rate
In the long run, unemployment is at the natural rate at any inflation rate
In the long run, unemployment falls to zero when inflation is high enough

items.q: Select every event that shifts the short-run Phillips curve to the right.
options: A rise in expected inflation
A rise in the price of oil used across the economy
A rise in government spending
A fall in consumer spending

items.q: A new technology sharply lowers energy costs for firms (a positive supply shock). What happens on the Phillips curve graph in the short run?
options: The SRPC shifts right: inflation and unemployment both rise
The economy moves up along the SRPC: inflation rises and unemployment falls
LRPC shifts right: the natural rate of unemployment rises
The SRPC shifts left: inflation and unemployment both fall

items.q: Which feature of the AD-AS model matches the long-run Phillips curve?
options: SRAS, which slopes up
LRAS, vertical at full-employment output
AD, which slopes down
The point where AD crosses SRAS in the short run

items.q: Use <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V = P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>. What is Kelvar's nominal GDP in Year 1, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You divided the money supply by velocity. Nominal GDP is the money supply times the number of times each dollar is spent: 500 x 4.

items.q: What is Kelvar's price level in Year 2? Give it as a number, where 1.0 means the base-year price level.

mistakes.why: You turned the formula upside down. Solve <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V = P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math> for P: P = (M x V) / Y = 2,200 / 2,000.
That is nominal GDP (M x V). Divide it by real GDP to get the price level.

items.q: By what percent did Kelvar's price level rise from Year 1 to Year 2?

mistakes.why: That is the Year 2 price level itself. The inflation rate is its percent change from Year 1, (1.1 - 1.0) / 1.0 x 100.
That is the change in the money supply in billions of dollars. Find the percent change in the price level.

items.q: In the table, the money supply grows 10 percent while velocity and real GDP stay the same. Which statement fits the quantity theory?
options: Real GDP rises 10 percent, and the price level is unchanged
The price level rises by the same 10 percent, and real output is unchanged
Velocity falls 10 percent, so nothing else changes
The price level falls 10 percent, since each dollar can now buy more output

items.q: Use the growth-rate form of the quantity theory, inflation = money growth + velocity growth - real output growth. About what inflation rate should Kaldo expect?

mistakes.why: You added real output growth. More output soaks up some of the new money, so subtract it: 40 + 0 - 2.
That is the money growth rate. Real output also grew 2 percent, which uses some of the new money: 40 - 2.

items.q: In the long run, how does Kaldo's fast money growth affect its real GDP?
options: Little or no lasting effect: real output depends on resources and technology
It raises real GDP by about 40 percent a year
It lowers real GDP by about 38 percent a year
It raises real GDP by the amount of the new money divided by velocity

items.q: Lenders in Kaldo come to expect this high inflation. What happens to the nominal interest rates they charge on new loans?
options: They fall, because there is more money available to lend
They stay the same, because the real interest rate is unchanged
They rise, because lenders add expected inflation to the real return they want
They fall to zero, because money loses value too quickly to lend

items.q: Suppose Kaldo slows money growth to 2 percent a year, with velocity steady and real GDP still growing 2 percent. About what inflation rate follows in the long run?
options: About 2 percent
About 4 percent
About 38 percent
About 0 percent

items.q: A country's nominal GDP is 16 trillion dollars and its money supply is 2 trillion dollars. What is the velocity of money?

mistakes.why: You divided money by nominal GDP. Velocity is nominal GDP divided by the money supply: 16 / 2.

items.q: What does the velocity of money measure?
options: How many times a year the average dollar is spent on final goods and services
How fast the central bank adds new money to the economy
How quickly prices rise over a year
How many times a new deposit is lent and re-lent through the whole banking system

items.q: An economy starts at full employment. The central bank increases the money supply once, and over time nominal wages adjust. Shift both curves that move and mark the new long-run equilibrium.

key.because: more money (AD) and then higher nominal wages (SRAS)

slips.LRAS: Money does not change the economy's resources or technology, so LRAS stays at full-employment output.

items.q: A central bank permanently raises the money supply. Which of these changes in the long run?
options: Real GDP
The natural rate of unemployment
The real interest rate
The price level

items.q: Why can a rise in the money supply raise real GDP in the short run but not in the long run?
options: Velocity doubles in the short run and then falls to zero
Nominal wages and some prices adjust slowly, so output can rise until they catch up
The central bank takes the money back out in the long run
LRAS shifts right in the short run and back left in the long run

items.q: The money supply grows faster than real output for many years. Select every variable that ends up higher because of it.
options: The price level
Nominal GDP
Real GDP
The unemployment rate

items.q: Velocity rises because people start paying with cards and spend money faster. If the money supply and real GDP stay the same, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises, because M x V is now larger while Y is unchanged
It falls, because money is spent faster and so is worth more
It stays the same, because the money supply did not change
It rises by exactly the rise in the money supply

items.q: Build the long-run chain from fast money growth to inflation.

specific.frame: The money supply grows faster, so nominal spending (M x V) ___. Velocity is steady and real output is set by ___, so the ___ rises, and ___ is unchanged in the long run.
specific.model: The money supply grows faster, so nominal spending (M x V) rises. Because velocity is steady and real output is set by resources and technology, the price level rises, which means higher inflation, and real GDP is unchanged in the long run.

spending.label: Nominal spending
options: rises
falls

why.1: More money times the same velocity is more spending, not less.

because.label: What sets real output
options: resources and technology
the money supply

why.1: In the long run output depends on productive capacity; that is what money neutrality means.

price.label: What rises
options: price level
velocity of money

why.1: Velocity is assumed steady; the price level absorbs the extra money.

output.label: What is unchanged
options: real GDP
nominal GDP

why.1: Nominal GDP equals M x V, so it rises with the money supply.

items.q: What is a government's budget deficit?
options: The total amount the government owes from past borrowing
The amount by which its outlays exceed its tax revenue in one year
The amount by which imports exceed exports in one year
The amount by which the government's tax revenue exceeds its outlays in one year

items.q: What is Brenna's budget balance in Year 2, in billions of dollars? Use a negative number for a deficit.

mistakes.why: The size is right but the sign is not: outlays are larger than revenue, so the balance is negative, a deficit of 60.
You added revenue and outlays. The balance is revenue minus outlays: 800 - 860.

items.q: How much does Brenna owe at the end of Year 3, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You added the Year 3 surplus to the debt. A surplus pays some debt off: 1,200 + 90 + 60 - 30.
You subtracted the deficits. Deficits are borrowed, so they add to the debt.

items.q: In which year did Brenna's national debt fall?
options: Year 2
Year 4
Year 3
Year 1

items.q: Brenna passed no new tax or spending law in Year 4, yet its deficit jumped to 130. What is the most likely reason?
options: A recession cut tax revenue and raised transfer payments through automatic stabilizers
An economic boom raised tax revenue faster than outlays
The central bank raised the money supply, which raised outlays
A budget surplus in Year 3 raised the interest owed in Year 4

items.q: Is the headline correct?
options: Yes: a smaller deficit means the debt is now 30 billion dollars smaller
No: the deficit fell, but the 50 billion borrowed this year still adds to the debt
Yes: a deficit and a debt are two names for the same thing
No: a smaller deficit makes the debt rise faster than it did before

items.q: How does Tarvia's government pay for its 50 billion dollar deficit?
options: It borrows, by selling government bonds
It raises the reserve requirement for banks
It cuts transfer payments by 50 billion dollars
It records the deficit as an export to other countries

items.q: Tarvia wants to move toward a balanced budget. Which action does that, and what does it do to AD?
options: Raising government spending, which shifts AD right
Cutting income taxes, which shifts AD left
Raising transfer payments, which shifts AD left
Raising income taxes, which shifts AD left

items.q: A government spends 4.5 trillion dollars (including transfers and interest) and collects 3.9 trillion dollars in taxes this year. How large is its budget deficit, in trillions of dollars? Give the size as a positive number.

mistakes.why: You added outlays and revenue. The deficit is the gap between them: 4.5 - 3.9.

items.q: During a recession, a legislature cuts taxes and raises spending to close the gap. What happens to the budget?
options: The deficit shrinks, because the policy raises output
The national debt falls, because the economy recovers
The deficit grows (or a surplus shrinks)
Nothing changes, because the two policies cancel out

items.q: Which statement correctly compares a budget deficit with the national debt?
options: A deficit is a flow over one year; the debt is a stock, the total owed at a point in time
A deficit is the total owed; the debt is the amount borrowed this year
A deficit is owed to foreigners; the debt is owed to citizens
A deficit is measured in percent; the debt in dollars

items.q: Interest rates on new government bonds rise. With no change in tax law or programs, what happens to the deficit over the next few years?
options: It shrinks, because higher rates bring the government more revenue
It grows, because interest on the debt is part of government outlays
It stays the same, because interest is not part of the budget
It disappears, because higher rates lower the price of existing bonds

items.q: Select every change that, by itself, makes a government's budget deficit larger.
options: A recession that lowers income tax collections
A rise in unemployment benefits paid as more people lose jobs
A rise in tax rates on income
A cut in spending on government programs

items.q: A government runs a balanced budget this year. What happens to the national debt?
options: It falls to zero, because a balanced budget pays off what is owed
It rises by the amount of tax revenue collected
It falls by the amount of government spending
It stays about the same: no new borrowing, no repayment

items.q: Build the chain from a recession to a larger national debt.

specific.frame: In a recession, incomes fall, so tax revenue ___ and transfer payments ___. The budget deficit ___, the government sells more ___, and the national debt ___.
specific.model: In a recession, incomes fall, so tax revenue falls and transfer payments rise. As a result the budget deficit grows, the government sells more bonds to borrow the difference, and the national debt rises.

change.label: Tax revenue
options: falls
rises

why.1: Lower incomes and profits mean less tax is collected.

link.label: Transfer payments
options: rise
fall

why.1: More people qualify for unemployment benefits and other transfers in a recession.

direction.label: The deficit
options: grows
shrinks

why.1: Lower revenue and higher outlays widen the gap.

tool.label: What the government sells
options: bonds
reserves

why.1: The government borrows by selling bonds; reserves are bank balances at the central bank.

trend.label: The debt
options: rises
falls

why.1: Each year's deficit is added to the debt.

items.q: Country X and Country Y each have a national debt of 500 billion dollars. Country X's GDP is 2,000 billion dollars a year and Country Y's is 500 billion dollars. Which statement compares the two debts best?
options: The two debts are equally heavy, since the dollar amounts match
Country Y's debt is easier to carry, since its economy is smaller
Country X's debt is lighter: 25% of its GDP against 100%
Neither country has a debt, since neither one reports a deficit

items.q: Label the axes and both curves of the loanable funds market graph.
A government increases its budget deficit and borrows to pay for it. Show the effect on the loanable funds market and mark the new equilibrium.

slips.SLF: The deficit raises the real interest rate either way: the demand for loanable funds shifts right (the government borrows more), or the supply shifts left (public saving falls). Shifting supply right would lower it.

items.q: A government that had been borrowing every year moves to a balanced budget and stops borrowing. Show the effect on the loanable funds market and mark the new equilibrium.

slips.SLF: A smaller deficit lowers the real interest rate either way: the demand for loanable funds shifts left (the government borrows less), or the supply shifts right (public saving rises). Shifting supply left would raise it.

items.q: While the government keeps borrowing, households decide to save a larger share of their incomes. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

slips.DLF: Saving is the source of loanable funds, so more saving shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: The graph shows Garrow's loanable funds market after its government increased its borrowing. What happened to the real interest rate?
options: It fell, because the government added funds to the market
It rose, because the supply of loanable funds decreased
It rose, because the demand for loanable funds increased
It stayed the same, because the quantity of funds also rose

items.q: The total quantity of loanable funds is larger on the graph. Why does private investment in Garrow still fall?
options: The government takes part of the larger quantity, and at the higher real rate private borrowers want less
Private investment rises, because the total quantity of funds rose
Savers lend less at the higher real rate, so there is less to invest
Firms invest less because the government's spending lowers their costs

items.q: If Garrow keeps borrowing this way for many years, what happens to its capital stock and potential output?
options: Both grow faster, because government spending replaces private investment
Both grow more slowly than they would have, because private investment is lower
The capital stock grows faster but potential output grows more slowly
Neither changes, since the borrowing affects interest rates rather than real output

mistakes.why: You left out the crowded-out investment. The net change in spending is 100 - 40 = 60, then times the multiplier of 5.
That is the net change in spending before the multiplier. Multiply it by 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5.

items.q: Build the crowding-out chain for Ferro.

supply

options: rises
falls

options: falls
rises

options: slowly
quickly

items.q: A new technology raises productivity in both industries. Shift the PPC to show the effect.
Place point X to show an economy in a recession, with unemployed workers and idle factories.

slips.AD: Training and equipment raise what the economy can produce; that is LRAS. A change in spending would shift AD.
slips.SRAS: Training and modern equipment raise the economy's long-run capacity, so LRAS must shift right. Shifting SRAS right as well, for lower costs, is accepted; shifting SRAS alone is not.

the price level

options: out
in

items.q: Years later, the finished highways cut shipping times and costs for firms across the economy. Shift the curve that shows the long-run effect on productive capacity.
